title: Rest isn't failure
hook: the World Health Organization lists burnout as a workplace phenomenon (2019)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Csikszentmihalyi, who named flow: challenge meeting skill until time disappears. Your line was absorbed. Today, the other side of the coin, when work empties you instead.

Burnout can sound like a personal weakness, something whispered about a colleague who couldn't keep up. Then the World Health Organization put it in its international classification of diseases, the big reference doctors use to name what they see. It isn't listed there as an illness. It's listed as a phenomenon of work: something that happens to people because of how they work. That wording moves the question. Not what's wrong with you, but what's been happening to you. Today: burnout.
screen: `A WHISPERED WEAKNESS?` → `A PHENOMENON OF WORK.` → `WHAT'S BEEN HAPPENING TO YOU.`

segments.voice: First, the description. The World Health Organization describes burnout as coming from chronic stress at work that hasn't been successfully managed. It names three marks: feeling depleted or exhausted; growing mental distance from your job, or feeling negative and cynical about it; and a sense that you're getting less done. It doesn't call burnout laziness, or a lack of faith, or a flaw in character. Second, an old story that fits. In the Hebrew Bible, the prophet Elijah, after a great contest and a death threat, runs into the wilderness, sits under a tree and asks to die. What happens next is not a lecture. He sleeps. An angel touches him and says, "Arise and eat." There's bread and water. He sleeps again, and eats again. Only after that does the journey go on. The first answer to his despair is rest and food. Third, a teacher who called a halt. In the Gospel of Mark, Jesus's followers come back so busy that, the text says, they had no time even to eat. And he tells them, "Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while." In that story, stepping away is not abandoning the work. It's part of it. Fourth, what this means on a Tuesday. If you are worn down to nothing, rest isn't the opposite of doing well. It may be what lets anything else happen. And if burnout is a phenomenon of work, the fix may also need to change the work, not only the worker. Rest is where that thinking can start.
screen: `THREE MARKS OF BURNOUT.` · `ELIJAH SLEEPS AND EATS.` · `REST A WHILE.` · `REST LETS THE WORK GO ON.` · then, large: `REST ISN'T FAILURE.`

segments.voice: For these two minutes you're off duty: let your shoulders drop and your hands go loose, close your eyes if you can, and breathe out a little longer than you breathe in. If a task comes to mind, picture setting it down on a table beside you; it'll still be there later. You don't have to achieve anything, not even a good meditation; just rest, the way Elijah slept under the tree.
Burnout. The World Health Organization's name for what chronic, unmanaged stress at work does to a person. Today's word.
Your line: arise and eat. Rest is part of the work, not a failure at it. Day nine hundred nine.

howItsDone: People recovering from burnout often combine real breaks with changes to the work itself; some religious communities also keep regular times of rest and retreat.

chat.says: I'm exhausted and cynical about my job lately. Does that just mean I'm lazy?
options: No. The WHO links burnout to unmanaged stress at work, not to a flaw in character.
Yes, mostly. Burnout is what happens when someone doesn't try hard enough.
No, it's just a phase; pushing through harder is the best way out of it.
chat.meaning: The WHO lists burnout as a phenomenon of work, from chronic unmanaged stress, not laziness or a flaw; even Elijah's first answer was rest and food.

phenomenon of work.meaning: something that happens to people because of how they work

notes: The ICD-11 description is paraphrased; check the three dimensions (exhaustion; mental distance, negativism or cynicism; reduced professional efficacy) and that it is classed as an occupational phenomenon, not a medical condition. The index's year is left out of the voice under the claims rule.
Elijah story (1 Kings 19:1–8) is paraphrased apart from 'Arise and eat.' (verse 5). 'After a great contest' refers to Mount Carmel in chapter 18; check the framing.
Mark 6:31 'they had no leisure so much as to eat' is paraphrased in the voice as 'no time even to eat'.
The script avoids medical advice; a reviewer may want to add a line pointing people with severe burnout to professional help.
